claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure.
The alloy is processed by arc melting followed by controlled annealing.
The resulting structure contains engineered nanograin regions embedded in a coarser-grained matrix.
The hierarchical structure contains well-defined interphase boundaries.
Grain-size distributions, interphase-boundary characteristics, and nano-to-micron heterogeneities can be integrated as descriptors in a data-driven reduced-order model.
The combination of nanograin regions, coarse-grained phases, and interphase boundaries governs local deformation in HfNbTiVAl10.
The hierarchical microstructure governs dislocation motion.
The hierarchical microstructure governs crack initiation.
Focusing computation on dominant structural mediators can capture elastic deformation, plastic yielding, and fracture initiation without representing the full detailed microstructure.
The reduced complexity decreases computational overhead and produces faster convergence.
Data-driven calibration improves predictive accuracy relative to traditional continuum or atomistic simulations.
The reduced-order model will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior 30–50% faster than established full-scale simulations.
The model will reduce prediction errors by approximately 10–20% for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture metrics.
Established full-system finite-element and molecular-dynamics simulations average the entire microstructure without targeted emphasis on hierarchical features.
Departures from the designed hierarchical microstructure due to inhomogeneous processing or aging may cause the model to fail.
Extreme strain rates may cause the model to fail because additional dynamic effects become dominant.
Insufficient microstructural descriptors may prevent the model from capturing emergent complex phenomena.
The exact numerical gains in speed and accuracy are uncertain until the model is calibrated against comprehensive experimental data.
The model is falsified if its predictions differ from independent measurements by more than 15%.
The model is falsified if it does not provide at least a 10% accuracy improvement and a 30% computational-efficiency increase over established full-scale simulations.
